newsitem.title: USA: IMF says Thailand rescue package fits the bill.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Thailand rescue package fits the bill.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday gave a ringing endorsement to the Thai government's efforts to stabilise the Southeast Asian nation's economy and its ailing currency, the baht.

"I greatly welcome today's important announcement by Thai authorities aimed at overcoming present economic problems in Thailand through the introduction of a comprehensive package of policies," IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said in a statement.

The Thai government earlier on Tuesday unveiled a set of reforms to help ease its economic woes after the baht came under fierce attack from investors worried about the country's excessive foreign borrowing and frail banking system. The baht has lost 20 percent of its value since it was allowed to float on July 2.
Camdessus commended the Thai government's package for its focus on "immediate and sweeping measures" to keep the country's battered financial system afloat.

"I found particularly appropriate the adoption of a comprehensive restructuring of troubled financial institutions, as this is essential to lay the basis for the re-establishment of a sound financial sector," he said.

The programme is aimed at securing some $15 billion in loans from the IMF and foreign nations. It includes the suspension of operations of more than half of Thailand's finance companies, a three percentage point rise in value-added tax and strict monetary and fiscal targets for the next few years.

Camdessus said an IMF team was in Thailand to assess the government's plan and to work with Bangkok on how it could be developed into "a multi-year adjustment programme that could be supported by IMF resources."
He added he expected such a programme to be presented to the IMF Executive Board for approval shortly.

Camdessus said he was in close touch with governments in the region and international financial institutions to put together a supplementary financing package to support the Thai government's measures.
"I am confident that today's strong actions by Thailand and the financial support that could be extended to it will decisively contribute to stability in financial markets in Asia," he said.

The fall-out from the Thai crisis affected other countries in the region, including the Philippines, which was also forced to devalue its currency and borrow from the IMF. ((Washington newsroom, 202-898 8377))
